A threat is anything that could cause harm, a vulnerability is a weakness it could exploit, and risk is the likelihood of that happening multiplied by the impact on something of value. If any one of the three is absent, there is little or no risk, which is why an unpatched server on an isolated network can be lower risk than a patched one on the internet. Risk work begins by knowing what you have: an asset inventory, with owners and an idea of how important each asset is to the business. The business impact analysis then tells you which functions matter most, how long the business can survive without them and how much data it can afford to lose.

Once risks are identified, each gets a treatment. You can mitigate by adding controls, transfer by buying insurance or shifting responsibility by contract, avoid by dropping the risky activity, or accept by knowingly living with it. Transfer shifts the financial cost but not accountability or reputation. Whatever remains after treatment is residual risk, and someone with authority must formally accept it. Everything is recorded in a risk register with a named owner for every entry. When numbers are available, quantitative analysis helps justify spending. Single loss expectancy is asset value multiplied by exposure factor, annualized rate of occurrence is how many times a year the event is expected, and annualized loss expectancy is the first multiplied by the second. If a control reduces the annualized loss expectancy by more than it costs each year, it is worth buying.

Vulnerability management is the repeatable operational loop that finds weaknesses before attackers do. You scan, preferably with credentials so the scanner can read patch levels and settings from the inside, which gives more accurate results than a scan from outside. You validate findings because scanners produce false positives, then prioritize by real risk. The Common Vulnerability Scoring System gives a 0 to 10 severity rating and CVE gives each flaw a public name, but neither measures risk to your environment. Add asset value, exposure and whether the flaw is already being exploited, for example by checking the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Then you patch or apply compensating controls, rescan to confirm and report.

Penetration testing goes one step beyond scanning: an authorized tester tries to exploit weaknesses to show real impact. Black box testers start with nothing, gray box testers get something such as a standard user account, and white box testers get documentation and source code. Whatever the type, the first step is written authorization from someone entitled to give it, along with rules of engagement describing scope, targets, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and stop conditions. Testing without that paperwork can be a crime, however good the intentions.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to risk management? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think about whether to carry an umbrella. The threat is rain, the vulnerability is that your suit is not waterproof, and the risk is the chance of a downpour on your walk multiplied by how bad a ruined suit would be. You can mitigate by carrying a coat, transfer by dry-cleaning insurance, avoid by working from home, or accept getting a little wet. If a 200 dollar suit would be half ruined once every two years, a 10 dollar umbrella is plainly worth it, and that is annualized loss expectancy thinking. A weather forecast is your threat intelligence, and a doctor checking your lungs is the scan; the test of whether the cold actually makes you ill is the penetration test.
commonTraps: CVSS measures technical severity, not risk to your organization. Two vulnerabilities with the same score can deserve very different priorities.
Insurance transfers the financial impact only. It does not transfer accountability, legal duties or reputational damage.
A vulnerability scan only finds potential weaknesses; a penetration test proves they can be exploited and needs prior written authorization.
Single loss expectancy is not annualized. Multiply by the annualized rate of occurrence to reach ALE, and compare ALE reduction to the control's yearly cost.
lessons.scenario: A retailer's quarterly scan lists 400 findings. The security practitioner removes false positives by running credentialed scans, then ranks the rest using exposure and asset value, not CVSS alone. A critical flaw on the internet-facing payments portal that is being exploited elsewhere jumps to the top; an equally scored flaw on an isolated lab server is scheduled for the next maintenance window. After patching, a rescan confirms closure and the results go into a short report with time-to-remediate trends.
lessons.onTheJob: Do not let scanning become a ritual of printing reports no one reads. Agree remediation timeframes with system owners in advance, such as days for actively exploited internet-facing flaws and weeks for lower risk items, and track the numbers publicly. Keep an exceptions register for systems that cannot be patched, with a compensating control, an owner and an expiry date. Schedule scans so they do not knock over fragile legacy equipment, and always scan authenticated where you can. Before any penetration test, get the rules of engagement signed, make sure the operations team knows who to call if something breaks, and agree what happens if the testers find evidence of a real attacker. Document risk acceptances in writing; verbal acceptance disappears the day the person leaves.

lessons.title: Monitoring, Logging and Detection
lessons.summary: How to collect, protect and analyze logs, and how SIEM, intrusion detection, baselines and threat intelligence turn raw data into detections.
lessons.reading:
You cannot investigate what you did not record, and you cannot trust a record that someone could edit. Good logging therefore has four parts. First, decide what to log: authentication successes and failures, privilege use, changes to configuration, access to sensitive data, security tool alerts, and network device and application events. Second, send logs off the host in near real time to a central, protected store, so an attacker who takes over a machine cannot erase the trail. Third, synchronize every clock with NTP and agree on a time zone, because correlating events across systems with drifting clocks produces timelines that mislead. Fourth, retain logs for as long as policy, regulation and investigations require, and protect them with integrity controls and restricted access.

A security information and event management platform, or SIEM, collects logs from many sources, normalizes them into a common format, correlates events and raises alerts. Its power comes from correlation: one failed login is noise, but fifty failed logins across ten accounts followed by a success from a new country is a story. A SIEM is only as good as the sources feeding it and the tuning of its rules. Poor tuning creates alert fatigue, where analysts stop looking, and weak coverage leaves blind spots. Both need constant care.

Detection technologies each have strengths. An intrusion detection system observes and alerts, usually fed by a span port or tap, while an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can block. Signature-based detection recognizes known bad patterns reliably but cannot see new attacks. Anomaly or behavior-based detection compares activity with a baseline of normal and can spot unknown attacks at the cost of more false positives. That is why a baseline taken while the environment is known to be clean is valuable, and why you re-baseline after legitimate major changes. On endpoints, endpoint detection and response tools record process, file and network activity and let analysts investigate and contain a host remotely.

Every detection system makes two kinds of mistakes. A false positive is an alert on something harmless; it wastes time. A false negative is a missed attack; it creates false confidence, and it is usually the more dangerous error. Tuning moves the balance but never removes it, so layered detection, regular testing of detections and threat hunting matter. Threat intelligence feeds this work with indicators of compromise such as hashes, domains and addresses, but those go stale quickly. Descriptions of attacker behavior, such as those in the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base, last much longer and make better detection ideas.

Finally, monitoring supports management decisions. Continuous monitoring replaces annual snapshots with near real-time visibility of assets, vulnerabilities, configuration and events. Audits compare practice with a standard, ideally by an independent party. Reports to leadership work best when they show outcomes, such as mean time to detect and mean time to contain, rather than counts of alerts or gigabytes of logs collected.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security monitoring? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine a shopping centre. Security cameras and door counters generate raw data, which is the logs. The control room that watches every screen together, notices that the same person has tried three different back doors, and phones the guards is the SIEM. A guard standing at a door who can tackle intruders is an intrusion prevention system, and a guard in the control room who only radios what they see is detection. Knowing what a normal Tuesday looks like is the baseline, so an unusual crowd at 3 a.m. stands out, and a wanted poster showing last month's thief's face is an indicator of compromise.
commonTraps: An IDS only alerts, and an IPS blocks. Only a device placed inline can block traffic; a span port copy cannot.
A false negative, a missed real attack, is usually more dangerous than a false positive, so do not tune alerts down until real events disappear.
Unsynchronized clocks break correlation. If an event timeline looks wrong, check time first.
A SIEM does not create visibility by itself. Without relevant log sources and tuned rules it produces little useful detection.
lessons.scenario: An analyst notices that two servers' logon events are several minutes out of order, which makes a suspected intrusion timeline impossible to build. The cause is an unsynchronized clock. After fixing NTP, the SIEM correlation shows many failed logons across different accounts from one address, then a success, which points to password spraying. The analyst enriches the alert with threat intelligence, isolates the affected account and tunes the rule so the same pattern raises a higher-priority alert in future.
lessons.onTheJob: Start small and concrete: pick ten use cases, such as impossible travel, new administrator accounts and disabled logging, and make sure each one is collected, parsed and alerting before expanding. Test detections regularly with simulated attacks, because a rule that has never fired may be silently broken. Protect the logging pipeline itself; alert when a host stops sending logs, since attackers often switch off logging first. Keep a written runbook for each alert type so a tired analyst at 3 a.m. knows what to check and when to escalate. Review retention against legal advice, because keeping everything forever creates cost and discovery risk, while deleting too soon destroys evidence. And report outcomes, not activity, so leadership can see whether detection is actually improving.

lessons.title: Incident Response, Forensics and Recovery
lessons.summary: The incident lifecycle, how to collect evidence without destroying it, and how business continuity, disaster recovery and backups restore operations.
lessons.reading:
An event is anything observable on a system or network; an incident is an event, or group of events, that actually or potentially harms security or breaks policy. Most alerts are events and never become incidents, so the first skill is triage: judge scope, affected assets, data sensitivity and business impact, then assign a severity that drives urgency and escalation. The accepted lifecycle has six stages. Preparation builds the plan, tools, contacts and trained team before anything happens. Detection and analysis confirm what is occurring. Containment stops the spread. Eradication removes the cause: malware, persistence mechanisms, rogue accounts and the vulnerability that let the attacker in. Recovery returns systems to service from known-good sources and watches for recurrence. Post-incident activity, the lessons-learned review, feeds improvements back into preparation. 

Containment decisions are where beginners hurt themselves. The instinct to pull the plug destroys memory contents, running processes and network connections, which are exactly the evidence you need. Isolate the host from the network instead, by switch port, host firewall or endpoint isolation, and keep it powered. During recovery, restoring from a backup taken after the compromise just reinstalls the attacker, so confirm the backup predates the intrusion and that the entry point is closed first.

If evidence may be needed for HR, regulators or court, forensic discipline matters. Collect in order of volatility: registers and cache, memory, network state and processes, disk, then remote logs and archives. Take a bit-for-bit image of storage through a write blocker, record a cryptographic hash of the original and the copy to show they match, and do all analysis on the copy. Maintain the chain of custody: a written record of who held the evidence, when, where and why, with every transfer signed. A gap does not prove tampering but it gives the other side something to argue. When litigation is reasonably expected, legal counsel issues a legal hold that suspends routine deletion, including log rotation and backup overwrites.

Recovery planning starts with the business impact analysis. Maximum tolerable downtime is how long a function can be out before harm becomes unacceptable. The recovery time objective is the target for restoring service and must be shorter than that limit. The recovery point objective is the most data, measured in time, that you can afford to lose and decides how often you back up or replicate. A hot site is ready within minutes or hours at the highest cost, a warm site has hardware but needs data and configuration restored, and a cold site offers space and power only. Choose the cheapest option that still meets the stated objectives.

Backups come in three common types. Full backups copy everything. Incremental backups copy changes since the last backup of any kind, so they are quick to make, but a restore needs the full backup plus every incremental in order. Differential backups copy changes since the last full backup, so a restore needs just the full backup and the latest differential. Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, because ransomware hunts for backup repositories, and test restores regularly.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to incident response? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of how a good crew handles a kitchen fire. Training and extinguishers in the right places are preparation. Noticing smoke and working out whether it is the toaster or the fryer is detection and analysis. Shutting the door and cutting the gas stops the spread, which is containment, and you do not throw out the burned pan until the investigator has photographed it. Eradication is removing whatever caused the fire, recovery is rebuilding the kitchen and reopening, and the review afterwards asks why the alarm was slow. The restaurant's insurance paperwork, showing who touched what and when, is the chain of custody.
commonTraps: Do not power off a compromised machine first. Isolate it from the network and capture volatile data before anything else.
The recovery time objective must fit inside the maximum tolerable downtime, and the recovery point objective, not the RTO, decides backup frequency.
Restoring an incremental chain needs the full backup plus every incremental; a differential restore needs only the full plus the latest differential.
Choose the cheapest recovery site that meets the stated objectives. A hot site is not automatically the right answer.
Post-incident reviews are blameless and aimed at improving controls, not at punishing the person who made the error.
lessons.scenario: At 7:40 on a Monday an analyst sees a workstation renaming files and showing a ransom note. She isolates it from the network, keeps it powered, captures memory and escalates to the incident commander. Backup administrators disconnect the backup repository from the domain while the team confirms the entry point was a phishing email. Systems are rebuilt from clean images and data restored from a copy that predates the infection, with the records database restored first because the business impact analysis ranks it highest. A week later the team meets to update detection rules and the phishing training.
lessons.onTheJob: Print the plan and keep an offline copy, because the day you need it your file server may be the thing that is encrypted. Know your three phone numbers before the incident: legal counsel, insurer and law enforcement liaison. Put a decision tree in the plan for the things people argue about under stress, such as when to isolate a production system and who can authorize it. Practise with tabletop exercises that include executives, because the hardest decisions, like whether to pay a ransom, belong to them and should not be debated for the first time during an attack. Treat backups as a product with an owner: test restores quarterly, time them against the recovery time objective and keep one copy that production credentials cannot touch. Record every action with a timestamp as you go; memory is unreliable at 3 a.m.

lessons.title: Cryptography in Practice
lessons.summary: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing, signatures, certificates, TLS and the key management habits that decide whether any of it actually protects you.
lessons.reading:
Cryptography gives you four useful properties: confidentiality (only intended parties can read), integrity (changes are detected), authentication (you know who produced it) and non-repudiation (they cannot deny it). Different tools provide different properties, and most exam questions are about matching the tool to the property. Symmetric encryption, such as the Advanced Encryption Standard, uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and suits large amounts of data, but the two parties must somehow share the key safely. Asymmetric encryption, such as RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, uses a mathematically linked pair: a public key anyone may have and a private key kept secret. It solves key distribution and enables signatures, but it is much slower. Real systems combine them: asymmetric methods agree on or protect a session key, and symmetric encryption protects the data.

Remember the key directions, because they are easy to reverse under pressure. To send a confidential message, encrypt with the recipient's public key, so only their private key can open it. To sign, hash the message and encrypt the hash with your own private key, so anyone can verify with your public key. A digital signature therefore gives integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation. A message authentication code such as HMAC mixes a shared secret into a hash. It proves integrity and that the sender knew the secret, but because both sides hold the secret it cannot give non-repudiation. A plain hash such as SHA-256 provides integrity only against accidental change, since anyone can recompute it after tampering. Hashing is one-way and keyless, so it is never reversed, and MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance.

Public key infrastructure answers the question of whose public key you really have. A certificate authority signs certificates that bind a public key to an identity, a registration authority vets requests, and clients trust the chain up to a root they already hold. Roots are kept offline in an HSM because losing one breaks everything beneath it. Certificates expire and can be revoked, either by a published certificate revocation list or by asking an online responder through OCSP. If a CA's key may be exposed, revoke it, rebuild with new keys and tell the people who rely on it. TLS uses all of this to protect data in transit. TLS 1.3 removes legacy ciphers and static RSA key exchange and requires ephemeral key exchange, giving forward secrecy, which means recorded traffic stays safe even if the server's long-term key is stolen later. Disable SSL and TLS 1.0 and 1.1.

Finally, strong algorithms are defeated by weak key handling. Generate keys with a good random source, store them in a hardware security module or managed key vault rather than beside the data they protect, limit who can use them, rotate them on a schedule and immediately after suspected compromise, back them up carefully, and destroy them at the end of their life. Keep separate protections for data at rest, in transit and in use, because encrypting a disk does nothing for traffic crossing the network.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to cryptography? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a padlock factory. Symmetric encryption is a single key that locks and unlocks a box: fast, but you must somehow get a copy of the key to your friend. Asymmetric encryption is like handing out open padlocks: anyone can snap one onto a box for you (encrypt with your public key), but only you hold the key that opens it. A signature is like a wax seal pressed with a stamp only you own, which everyone can recognize but nobody can forge. A hash is a fingerprint of the contents, and a certificate authority is the notary who confirms that this stamp really belongs to you.
commonTraps: Encrypt to a person with their public key; sign with your own private key. Reversing them is the most common mistake.
HMAC cannot provide non-repudiation because both parties know the key. Only an asymmetric signature can.
A hash alone does not protect against an attacker who can change the message and recompute the hash; you need a key (HMAC or signature).
ECB leaks patterns and should not be used. Authenticated modes like GCM are preferred, and nonces must never repeat with the same key.
lessons.scenario: Two offices must send nightly 500 GB backups and have no shared secret. The engineer uses an asymmetric exchange to agree on a session key, encrypts the data with AES in GCM mode, and signs each backup manifest so the receiver can verify origin and integrity. The root CA key for the company's internal certificates sits offline in an HSM, and the issuing CA's certificates are revocable through OCSP. When a developer leaves, the engineer rotates the keys that person could access.
lessons.onTheJob: Do not invent cryptography. Use well-reviewed libraries and current protocol versions, and treat any custom scheme as a defect. Keep an inventory of certificates and their expiry dates, because outages from expired certificates are far more common than attacks on algorithms. Automate renewals where you can, and alert at 30 days. Inspect configurations with a scanner to find old protocol versions and weak cipher suites, and retire them deliberately with monitoring so you know which clients break. Never store keys in source code or configuration files; use a vault and short-lived credentials. Plan for key loss as carefully as key theft: with no backup or escrow of a data-encryption key, encrypted data is simply gone. And watch the horizon on quantum computing, since long-lived secrets encrypted today may need post-quantum algorithms later.

lessons.title: Network and Communications Security
lessons.summary: How networks work, how they are attacked, and the segmentation, firewall, VPN, wireless and monitoring controls that defend them.
lessons.reading:
Start with the model. The seven-layer OSI model separates a network into physical signalling, data link (switches, MAC addresses, VLANs), network (routers, IP addresses), transport (TCP and UDP ports), session, presentation and application. The TCP/IP model groups these into four layers. Knowing where something sits tells you how to defend it: a switch-level attack such as ARP spoofing needs switch controls, a routing question belongs at layer 3, and a port or connection-state issue lives at layer 4. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable, built on a three-way handshake that SYN floods exploit by leaving connections half open, while UDP is connectionless, which makes spoofing and amplification attacks easier. 

Firewalls are the main traffic cops. A packet filter checks headers against rules, a stateful firewall tracks connections so replies are allowed automatically, and an application-layer or next-generation firewall inspects content and identifies applications and users. Rules are evaluated from the top and the first match wins, so specific rules go before general ones and the list ends in an explicit deny all. Firewalls work best with segmentation. A demilitarized zone holds internet-facing servers so that a compromised web server does not sit next to the database. VLANs separate broadcast domains but are not themselves a firewall: traffic between them must still be filtered. Microsegmentation applies the same idea to individual workloads, which matters when most traffic is server to server and never crosses a perimeter. Segmentation is the practical answer to lateral movement and ransomware spread.

Admission and identity come next. IEEE 802.1X is port-based network access control: a device authenticates through the switch or access point to a RADIUS server before the port passes traffic, which stops an unknown laptop gaining access by plugging into a wall socket. Wireless security has moved from WEP, which is broken, through WPA2 with AES to WPA3, which resists offline password guessing. Enterprise modes authenticate each person with 802.1X so access can be revoked individually. 

Remote connections use VPNs. A site-to-site tunnel joins two networks between gateways, usually IPsec in tunnel mode with ESP, which provides encryption and integrity; the Authentication Header authenticates but does not encrypt. A remote-access VPN joins one client, and split tunnelling sends only corporate traffic through it, trading load for exposure to a hostile local network. A modern alternative is Zero Trust Network Access, which grants per-application access after checking user and device instead of putting the user on the whole network. Administrators should reach devices through SSH, from a hardened jump host on a management network, with AAA through TACACS+ or RADIUS.

Attacks to recognize include denial of service, where distributed attacks use many sources and reflection abuses third parties, defended by rate limiting, SYN cookies and upstream scrubbing; man-in-the-middle and ARP spoofing, defended by dynamic ARP inspection, DHCP snooping and end-to-end encryption; and DNS abuse, including cache poisoning and tunnelling, where DNSSEC signs records but does not encrypt them.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to network security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture an office building. The street door with a guard is the perimeter firewall, and the visitor lobby is the DMZ where the public may wait but cannot wander upstairs. Internal doors that need a badge are VLANs and internal firewall rules: just because you are inside does not mean you can open the server room. The badge reader that checks who you are before the lift moves is 802.1X. An armoured van between two company buildings is a site-to-site VPN, and an executive carrying a locked briefcase through the airport is a remote-access VPN. A fake reception desk across the road that looks exactly like yours is an evil twin.
commonTraps: VLANs separate traffic but are not firewalls. Inter-VLAN routing still needs filtering.
NAT hides addresses but is not a security control; a stateful firewall provides the protection people credit to NAT.
AH authenticates but does not encrypt. ESP provides confidentiality and integrity, and tunnel mode is the usual choice between gateways.
A span port copy cannot block traffic; only an inline device can prevent, and its fail mode matters.
DNSSEC proves records are authentic but does not encrypt queries. Use DNS over TLS or HTTPS for privacy.
lessons.scenario: A company hosts a public web server, an email relay and an internal database. The engineer places the web and mail servers in a DMZ with firewall rules allowing only the specific ports and destinations required, and keeps the database in an internal VLAN that only the application tier can reach. Switch ports require 802.1X, wireless uses WPA3 Enterprise, and remote staff use ZTNA for the two internal web applications they need. Logs and flow records from the firewalls and switches go to the SIEM.
lessons.onTheJob: Review firewall rules every quarter and delete anything with no owner, no expiry or no recent hits; rule bases grow until nobody understands them. Always keep a console or out-of-band path to your network devices before you change access rules remotely, so you cannot lock yourself out. Back up device configurations and protect those backups, since they contain secrets. Test the failure modes of inline security devices before production: decide whether an overloaded IPS should fail open or closed and document who accepted that risk. When you introduce 802.1X, start in monitor mode and expect printers and cameras that cannot speak it, giving them a separate segment with tight rules. And remember that encryption cuts both ways: inspecting TLS lets you see malware but also gives your inspection device access to sensitive data, so scope and protect it carefully.

lessons.title: Systems, Endpoint, Cloud and Application Security
lessons.summary: Malware and attacker behavior, hardening and patching, endpoint and mobile controls, virtualization and cloud security, and secure application practices.
lessons.reading:
Malicious code is classified by how it spreads and what it does. A virus attaches to a host file and needs a user action to spread, a worm spreads by itself across networks, a trojan pretends to be legitimate software, ransomware locks or encrypts data for payment, a rootkit hides itself deep in the system and spyware gathers information quietly. Modern attackers increasingly avoid files completely. Fileless and living-off-the-land attacks run in memory and abuse legitimate tools such as PowerShell, so signature antivirus sees nothing, and defenders rely on behavior monitoring, script logging and endpoint detection and response. The most common way in remains social engineering: phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing and pretexting, countered by email filtering, MFA, authentication of mail domains with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and a reporting channel staff actually use.

Hardening reduces the attack surface. Start from a baseline such as a CIS Benchmark, remove software and services you do not need, close ports, disable default accounts, enable host firewalls and logging, and enforce disk encryption and secure boot. Patch management is the repeatable process of identifying, testing, deploying and verifying updates, with exceptions tracked and compensating controls for systems that cannot be patched. Application allowlisting, which permits only approved executables, is stronger than blocklisting for stable systems because it blocks the unknown by default. Endpoint detection and response adds visibility and remote containment, such as isolating a host, which ordinary antivirus lacks. For mobile devices, use device management with encryption, a work container and selective wipe, and keep Internet of Things devices on their own network segment.



Virtualization and cloud shift responsibility rather than removing it. A Type 1 hypervisor runs on hardware, a Type 2 hypervisor runs on a host operating system, and a compromise of the hypervisor affects every guest, so patch it and keep its management interface on an isolated network. Watch for VM sprawl, which is unmanaged and unpatched machines accumulating, and for VM escape, which is rare but severe. Containers share the host kernel, so run them as non-root from minimal, scanned images and never bake secrets into images. In the cloud, the shared responsibility model says the provider secures the cloud itself and the customer secures what it puts in the cloud. In infrastructure as a service the customer patches the guest operating system. In software as a service the provider manages almost the whole stack. In every model the customer owns its data, identities and configuration, and most cloud breaches come from misconfiguration such as publicly readable storage. 

Applications are the last layer. Build security into the whole development lifecycle: requirements, threat modelling in design, secure coding, automated static and dynamic testing, and controlled release. The OWASP Top Ten is a useful checklist of common web flaws. SQL injection is prevented with parameterized queries, cross-site scripting with output encoding and a content security policy, and cross-site request forgery with anti-forgery tokens.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to systems security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine running a block of rented flats. Hardening is fitting every flat with the same decent locks, taking out the unused back doors and fixing the broken window latches. Patching is doing the maintenance round when the manufacturer announces a faulty lock. An allowlist is a doorman with a guest list rather than a list of known burglars. Moving to the cloud is like renting space in someone else's building: the landlord keeps the lifts and the roof safe, but you must still lock your own flat and not leave the door propped open, which is where most break-ins actually happen.
commonTraps: A worm spreads on its own and a virus needs a host file and a user action. The exam keys on the propagation method.
In IaaS the customer, not the provider, patches the guest operating system. The provider handles the physical hosts and hypervisor.
Parameterized queries stop SQL injection, while output encoding stops cross-site scripting. They are not interchangeable.
Allowlisting blocks everything not approved; blocklisting only stops what is already known to be bad.
Cloud exposure is usually customer misconfiguration, not provider failure, so the customer is accountable for its own storage policies.
lessons.scenario: A company moves its warehouse application to rented virtual machines and finds the images unpatched for months, a storage bucket readable by anyone with the link, and warehouse staff reading company email on personal phones. The practitioner removes public access from the bucket, builds a hardened image with a patch schedule and logging, enrolls phones in device management with a work container, and enables behavior-based endpoint detection. Application teams get static and dynamic testing in their build pipeline.
lessons.onTheJob: Fix exposure before elegance: public storage, unpatched internet-facing systems and missing multi-factor authentication give attackers their easiest wins, so tackle those first. Build hardened images once and deploy them everywhere rather than hardening machines by hand, and keep the image pipeline patched so new systems are never born vulnerable. Use cloud configuration scanning continuously, not annually, and make logging a default in every new account or subscription. Insist on an owner for every virtual machine and a decommission date for temporary ones, since sprawl is where forgotten, unpatched servers live. For mobile and IoT, accept that you cannot secure everything on the device, so segment and monitor instead. Finally, teach developers with real examples from your own code reviews; a thirty-minute walkthrough of an injection flaw they wrote lands better than any slide deck.

cheatSheet.heading: Security concepts and practices (16%)
points: CIA triad: confidentiality (no unauthorized disclosure), integrity (no unauthorized change), availability (usable when needed). Non-repudiation and accountability need unique IDs, signatures and trustworthy logs.
Least privilege limits rights and time; need-to-know limits information; separation of duties splits a sensitive task so collusion is required; job rotation and mandatory vacation detect fraud.
Document hierarchy: policy (mandatory, high level), standard (mandatory, specific), procedure (mandatory steps), guideline (recommended).
Control functions: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, recovery. Control types: administrative, technical, physical. A question can ask for either axis.
ISC2 Code of Ethics canons in priority order: society and infrastructure, then act honorably and legally, then serve principals, then the profession.
Change management: request, assess, approve, test, implement with rollback, verify, document. Baselines detect drift. Life safety beats asset protection: exits fail safe.
Data lifecycle: classification is the owner's call; sanitize with clear, purge or destroy (NIST SP 800-88). Delete and quick format are not sanitization.

cheatSheet.heading: Access controls (15%)
points: Order: identification (claim), authentication (prove), authorization (permit), accounting (record). Factors: know, have, are. Two knowledge factors is not MFA.
Best MFA for privileged users is phishing-resistant: FIDO2 keys, passkeys or smart cards. SMS and push approvals are weaker.
Models: DAC (owner decides), MAC (labels set centrally), RBAC (job role), ABAC (attributes and context), rule-based (fixed rules for everyone).
SSO concentrates risk in the identity provider. SAML for enterprise web SSO, OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization (not authentication), OpenID Connect adds identity on OAuth.
Kerberos is ticket-based and needs clocks within about five minutes. RADIUS: UDP, encrypts password only. TACACS+: TCP, encrypts all, per-command authorization.
Lifecycle: provision from authoritative source, recertify regularly, deprovision fast. Disable first, delete later. Remove old roles on job change.
Passwords: salted slow hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2), screen against breached lists, no forced rotation without cause. Service accounts: vault, rotate, least privilege.

cheatSheet.heading: Risk identification, monitoring and analysis (15%)
points: Risk is likelihood times impact. Treatments: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept. Residual risk remains after controls and must be formally accepted.
SLE = asset value x exposure factor. ALE = SLE x ARO. A control is justified when it reduces ALE by more than it costs per year.
CVE names a flaw, CVSS scores severity, CWE classes the weakness. CVSS is not risk: add exposure, asset value and active exploitation (for example CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list).
Credentialed scans are more accurate; penetration tests prove exploitability and need written authorization and rules of engagement first. Black box no knowledge, gray partial, white full.
Logs: central, tamper-resistant, time-synchronized (NTP), retained per policy. SIEM correlates; its value depends on log sources and tuning.
Signature detection misses new attacks; anomaly detection needs a clean baseline and raises false positives. A false negative is usually worse than a false positive.
Continuous monitoring replaces annual snapshots. BIA comes before recovery strategy and defines criticality, MTD, RTO and RPO.

cheatSheet.heading: Incident response and recovery (14%)
points: Lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, post-incident (lessons learned). Event is observable; incident violates or threatens security.
Contain by isolating, not powering off, so memory survives. Do not restore a backup taken after the compromise. Fix the root cause before returning to service.
Forensics: order of volatility (registers and cache, RAM, network state, disk, remote logs and archives). Hash-verified bit-for-bit image, write blocker, analyze the copy, chain of custody always.
Legal hold suspends deletion when litigation is reasonably expected. Only designated spokespeople communicate externally; legal reviews notifications.
RTO must be less than MTD; RPO sets backup or replication frequency. Hot site fast and costly, warm needs data restore, cold takes days.
Backups: full; incremental needs full plus every incremental; differential needs full plus latest differential. Keep offline or immutable copies and test restores.
DR tests in rising realism: read-through, tabletop or walkthrough, simulation, parallel, full interruption. Parallel runs alongside production.

cheatSheet.heading: Cryptography (9%)
points: Symmetric (AES) is fast and shares one key; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses a key pair and solves key distribution. Real systems are hybrid.
Encrypt to someone with their public key; sign with your own private key; verify with the signer's public key. Digital signatures give non-repudiation; HMAC does not.
Hashes (SHA-256, SHA-3) give integrity only and are one-way. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collisions. Unkeyed hashes can be recomputed by an attacker.
Modes: never ECB; prefer authenticated modes like GCM; never reuse a nonce or IV with the same key.
PKI: CA signs certificates, RA vets, root kept offline, revocation by CRL or OCSP. Compromised CA key means revoke and rebuild trust.
TLS 1.3: forward secrecy mandatory, legacy ciphers removed. Disable SSL and TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Protect keys in an HSM or TPM and rotate them.

cheatSheet.heading: Network and communications security (16%)
points: Layers: switches layer 2, routers layer 3, TCP and UDP layer 4. SYN flood abuses the TCP handshake; mitigate with SYN cookies and rate limiting.
Firewalls: first match wins, specific before general, end with default deny. Stateful tracks connections; next-generation inspects applications and users.
Segment with DMZ, VLANs and microsegmentation to stop lateral movement. VLANs are not firewalls. Harden against VLAN hopping and ARP spoofing (DAI, DHCP snooping, port security).
IDS alerts (passive, span port); IPS blocks (inline, mind its fail mode). IPsec: ESP encrypts, AH does not, tunnel mode for gateways, IKE negotiates keys.

802.1X with RADIUS and EAP authenticates devices at the port or access point. WPA3 resists offline guessing; WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise gives per-user accountability. Hiding SSIDs and MAC filtering are not security.
Replace cleartext: SSH for Telnet, HTTPS for HTTP, SFTP for FTP, LDAPS for LDAP, SNMPv3 for SNMPv1 and v2c. DNSSEC signs DNS but does not encrypt it.
NAT is not a firewall. Split tunnelling sends only corporate traffic through the VPN. ZTNA gives per-application access instead of whole-network access.

cheatSheet.heading: Systems and application security (15%)
points: Malware: virus needs host and user action, worm self-spreads, trojan masquerades, rootkit hides, ransomware extorts. Fileless attacks abuse built-in tools and need behaviour-based detection (EDR).
Harden: baseline, remove unneeded services, patch, host firewall, logging. Application allowlisting beats blocklisting for stable systems.
Mobile: MDM or UEM with encryption, passcode, container and selective wipe; treat rooted or jailbroken devices as non-compliant. Isolate IoT devices on their own segment.
Cloud shared responsibility: customer always owns data, identities and configuration; guest OS patching is the customer's in IaaS. Most breaches are misconfiguration. CASB finds shadow IT.
Virtualization: patch the hypervisor, isolate its management network, control VM sprawl. Containers share the kernel: non-root, minimal scanned images, protect secrets.
Web: parameterized queries stop SQL injection; output encoding and content security policy stop cross-site scripting; anti-forgery tokens stop cross-site request forgery.
Email: SPF lists senders, DKIM signs, DMARC sets policy and reports. They authenticate domains and reduce spoofing but do not stop all phishing.

cheatSheet.heading: Quick discriminators that decide many questions
points: Whose job is it? Owner classifies and approves; custodian implements; the administrator does not reclassify.
Stop and preserve beats stop and destroy: isolate, do not power off; disable, do not delete; image, do not analyze the original.
Detective versus preventive: logs, cameras, reviews and audits detect; locks, encryption, MFA and segmentation prevent; visible monitoring deters.
Match the control to the state of the data: at rest means disk or database encryption, in transit means TLS, IPsec or SSH, in use means enclaves.
Cost-justify: the cheapest option that still meets the stated RTO, RPO or requirement beats the most powerful option.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: since 1 October 2025 the SSCP is computerized adaptive: 100 to 125 items in 2 hours, scored 0 to 1000 with 700 to pass. Multiple choice plus advanced item types.
Adaptive testing means item difficulty tracks your answers, so a run of hard questions is normal. You cannot go back to change answers, so decide and move on.
Budget about one minute per item. If a question is unclear, eliminate the two weakest options, pick the best remaining one and continue.

Practitioner questions ask what to do, usually BEST, FIRST or MOST appropriate. FIRST means the earliest step in the lifecycle (authorize before testing, contain before eradicate, assess before treat).
Choose answers that follow standards, preserve evidence, protect life safety first, apply least privilege and use the lowest-cost option that meets the stated requirement.
Read the last line of a scenario first to see what is being asked, then re-read the details. Watch for qualifiers like NOT, EXCEPT and BEST.
This mock uses a shorter fixed set of questions; treat 75 percent or more as a safe buffer, not an exact predictor of your scaled score.

madlibs.scenario: A bank installs a visible camera over its vault door. Because staff and criminals can see it, it acts as a {b1} control, and because it records who enters, it also works as a {b2} control. It does nothing to physically stop entry, so it is not a {b3} control.

options: deterrent
corrective
recovery
preventive
detective
compensating
preventive
detective
deterrent

madlibs.explanation: Visibility discourages (deterrent) and recording identifies what happened (detective). Only a lock, door or similar barrier is preventive, because it physically stops the event.

madlibs.scenario: A user types a username, which is {b1}. She then proves it with a password plus a code from a hardware key, which is {b2} because the factors come from different categories. Finally the system checks what she may open, which is {b3}.

options: identification
authentication
authorization
multi-factor authentication
single-factor authentication
federation
accounting
authorization
identification

madlibs.explanation: A claimed identity is identification, proof across knowledge and possession factors is multi-factor authentication, and deciding permitted actions is authorization. Accounting is the recording of what the user then did.

madlibs.scenario: A server worth 100,000 dollars would lose half of its value in one flood, so the single loss expectancy is {b1}. Floods are expected once every four years, so the annualized rate of occurrence is {b2}. The annualized loss expectancy is therefore {b3}.

options: 50,000 dollars
100,000 dollars
25,000 dollars
12,500 dollars
25,000 dollars
200,000 dollars

madlibs.explanation: SLE is asset value times exposure factor, 100,000 times 0.5. ARO is 1 over 4, or 0.25 per year. ALE is SLE times ARO, 50,000 times 0.25, which is 12,500 dollars a year.

madlibs.scenario: A file server is protected by a full backup on Sunday and a backup of changes since Sunday on each other night. Because each night's backup grows until the next full backup, this is a {b1} strategy, and a restore needs the full backup plus the {b2}. If each night instead copied only changes since the previous night, a restore would need the full backup plus {b3}.

options: differential
incremental
mirror
most recent differential
oldest differential only
every differential
only the last incremental
every incremental in order
nothing else

madlibs.explanation: Differentials hold everything changed since the last full backup, so only the latest is needed. Incrementals hold only changes since the previous backup of any kind, so all of them are needed, in order.

madlibs.scenario: To send Bob a message only he can read, Alice encrypts it with Bob's {b1}. To prove a document came from her and was not altered, Alice creates a digital signature using her own {b2}. Bob checks that signature using Alice's {b3}.

options: public key
private key
session key
public key
private key
password hash
private key
public key
shared secret

madlibs.explanation: Confidentiality uses the recipient's public key because only the matching private key can decrypt. Signing uses the sender's private key, and anyone can verify with the corresponding public key.

madlibs.scenario: A sensor connected to a switch span port can watch traffic and raise alerts but cannot block it, so it is an {b1}. A device placed inline that can drop malicious packets is an {b2}. Because the inline device sits in the traffic path, its failure mode matters: if it fails {b3}, all traffic stops.

options: intrusion detection system
intrusion prevention system
proxy server
intrusion detection system
intrusion prevention system
network tap
open
closed
silent

madlibs.explanation: Passive monitoring through a span port is detection. Inline placement allows prevention. A fail-closed inline device blocks traffic when it fails, which protects security but risks an outage, whereas fail-open keeps traffic flowing without inspection.

madlibs.scenario: A company moves a database server to virtual machines rented from a cloud provider, a model called {b1}. Under the shared responsibility model the provider secures the physical hosts and hypervisor, while the customer must patch the {b2} and manage its own {b3}.

options: infrastructure as a service
software as a service
platform as a service
guest operating system
data centre generators
hypervisor firmware
data and access configuration
physical network cabling
building security

madlibs.explanation: Renting virtual machines is IaaS, where the customer owns everything above the hypervisor: the guest operating system, applications, data and identity and access configuration. Facilities and physical hosts stay with the provider.

sequences.prompt: Put these incident response phases in the correct order for a confirmed malware infection on a server.
steps: Preparation: plans, tools, contacts and training are already in place
Detection and analysis: confirm the alert is a real incident and scope it
Containment: isolate the affected systems to stop the spread
Eradication: remove the malware, persistence and the exploited weakness
Recovery: restore from known-good sources and monitor for recurrence
Post-incident activity: hold a lessons-learned review and update plans
sequences.explanation: Preparation precedes any incident. Detection and analysis confirm what is happening before action is taken, containment limits the damage while evidence is preserved, eradication removes the cause, recovery restores service, and the review feeds lessons back into preparation.

sequences.prompt: Order the evidence to collect from a live compromised host, from MOST volatile to LEAST volatile.
steps: CPU registers and cache
Contents of memory (RAM) and running processes
Network connections and routing state
Contents of the disk
Remote logs and archival backups
sequences.explanation: Evidence is collected in order of volatility because the most fleeting data disappears first. Registers and cache change by the instant, memory and process data vanish at power-off, network state is transient, disk contents persist, and remote logs and archives last longest.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps of a vulnerability management cycle for a monthly scan of production servers.
steps: Maintain an accurate inventory of assets to be scanned
Run an authorized, credentialed vulnerability scan
Validate the findings and rank them by risk, not by score alone
Test and deploy patches or apply compensating controls
Rescan to verify the fixes and report the results
sequences.explanation: You cannot scan what you do not know about, so the inventory comes first. Findings need validation and risk-based prioritization before remediation, and a rescan confirms that the fix worked and closes the loop.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps of a standard change management process in order.
steps: Submit a change request describing the reason, scope and risk
Assess impact and obtain approval from the change authority
Test the change in a non-production environment
Implement during an approved window with a rollback plan ready
Verify the result and update documentation and baselines
sequences.explanation: A change is requested, assessed and approved before it is tested, and it is tested before it is implemented. A rollback plan lets the team reverse a failed change, and verification and documentation keep baselines accurate.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for obtaining and deploying a TLS certificate for a public web server.
steps: Generate a key pair on the server and keep the private key protected
Create a certificate signing request containing the public key and identity
The certificate authority validates the request and signs the certificate
Install the certificate and the intermediate chain on the server
Monitor the expiry date and renew or revoke as needed
sequences.explanation: The private key is generated first and never leaves the server. The signing request carries only the public key, the authority validates and signs it, the server needs the whole chain to be trusted by clients, and certificates must be renewed or revoked over their lifecycle.

caseStudies.title: Harborview Clinic: Ransomware on a Monday Morning
caseStudies.scenario: Harborview Clinic runs about 200 workstations, two file servers and a records database. At 7:40 on Monday the on-call analyst sees an alert from the endpoint detection tool: a reception workstation is renaming thousands of files with a strange extension, and a ransom note has appeared on its desktop. Within minutes two shared folders on a file server show the same behaviour. The analyst's account on the backup server shows nightly backups completed successfully, but the backup server is a domain member, reachable from every workstation with the same credentials the attacker may have captured. The clinic's incident plan names an incident commander, lists contacts for legal counsel and the cyber insurer, and requires evidence to be preserved. The clinic must keep seeing patients, and its recovery objectives for the records database are a four-hour recovery time and 30 minutes of acceptable data loss. Executives are asking whether to simply pay the ransom to be back online quickly.

questions.question: What should the analyst do FIRST?
options: Isolate the affected workstation and file server from the network while preserving their state, and escalate to the incident commander
Power off every workstation in the clinic to stop encryption
Restore the file server from last night's backup immediately
Negotiate with the attackers to learn the ransom amount
questions.explanation: Containment limits the spread while keeping memory and disk evidence, and the incident commander coordinates the response. A mass power-off destroys volatile evidence and disrupts patient care, restoring before containment would be re-encrypted, and negotiating is a business and legal decision made later, not a technical first step.

questions.question: Which TWO actions protect the clinic's ability to recover? (Choose two.)
options: Disconnect or restrict access to the backup repository and verify a copy that production credentials cannot reach
Restore only after confirming the entry point is closed and the backup predates the compromise
Restore the records database onto the same compromised network segment right away
Delete the encrypted files to free disk space for restores
questions.explanation: Backups are a common ransomware target, so isolating them preserves recovery, and restoring before removing the cause or from an infected backup invites reinfection. Restoring onto the compromised segment risks re-encryption, and deleting encrypted files destroys evidence and possibly recoverable data.

questions.question: Paying the ransom is the technically correct next step because it guarantees the data will be restored.
questions.explanation: Paying does not guarantee working decryption and may carry legal and sanctions implications. Whether to pay is a management and legal decision made with counsel and insurer, after assessing backups, and it is not a substitute for containment and recovery.

questions.question: The records database has a four-hour recovery time and 30-minute data-loss limit. Nightly backups are the only copies. What does this MOST clearly show?
options: The backup strategy cannot meet the recovery point objective and needs more frequent replication or log shipping
The recovery time objective is too short and should be abandoned
Nightly backups satisfy the objective because they are tested weekly
The objectives only apply to the file servers
questions.explanation: Nightly backups can lose up to a day of data, far more than the 30-minute RPO, so the design needs continuous replication or frequent log backups. Objectives come from the business impact analysis and are not dropped because the design cannot meet them, and testing does not change how much data can be lost.

caseStudies.title: Northwind Logistics: Securing a Hybrid Environment
caseStudies.scenario: Northwind Logistics has recently moved its warehouse management application to virtual machines in a public cloud, while keeping its finance system on premises. A quick review by the new security practitioner finds several issues. A cloud storage bucket holding shipping manifests is readable by anyone with the link. The cloud virtual machines were built from an old image and have not been patched in months. Warehouse staff use personal phones to scan packages and read company email, with no device management. On the internal network, network engineers manage switches with Telnet and the switches still use their default passwords. Administrators log in to every server with one shared admin account. Logs from the cloud environment and on-premises servers are not collected anywhere. Management wants a prioritized plan that follows the shared responsibility model and reduces the most risk first, and has asked the practitioner to explain which problems belong to Northwind, which belong to the cloud provider, and which should be fixed this week rather than this quarter.

questions.question: According to the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating systems of the cloud virtual machines?
options: Northwind, because it rented infrastructure as a service
The cloud provider, because it owns the physical hosts
The hypervisor vendor
Northwind's internet service provider
questions.explanation: In IaaS the customer manages the guest operating system, applications and data, while the provider handles physical hosts and virtualization. The hypervisor vendor and the internet service provider have no responsibility for the tenant's guest systems.

questions.question: Which TWO actions should be taken FIRST because they address the highest and most immediate risks? (Choose two.)
options: Remove public access from the storage bucket holding the manifests
Replace shared admin logins with individual accounts and rotate the default switch passwords
Change the colour scheme of the warehouse application
Purchase a larger cloud storage tier for future growth
questions.explanation: Publicly readable data and shared or default administrative credentials expose data and destroy accountability right now, and they are cheap to fix. Cosmetic changes and storage tiers do not reduce risk.

questions.question: Warehouse staff use personal phones for company email. Which control BEST protects company data while respecting personal use?
options: Enrol the phones in mobile device management with a work container, encryption, a passcode and selective wipe
Ban smartphones in the warehouse entirely and issue nothing
Allow email forwarding to personal accounts for convenience
Request that staff remember to log out each night
questions.explanation: Device management with a managed container protects corporate data and allows removal of just that data when someone leaves. A ban without alternatives disrupts work and tends to be ignored, forwarding to personal accounts loses control, and reminders are not a technical control.

questions.question: Collecting logs from cloud and on-premises systems into one protected, time-synchronized location would improve both detection and incident investigation.
questions.explanation: Central, tamper-resistant logging with consistent time supports correlation, alerting and forensic timelines, and it keeps evidence safe if a host is compromised.

compare.scenario: A data centre's electronic door locks lose power during a building fire alarm. The facilities team must choose the default lock behaviour for the personnel exit doors. Which is the better design?
compare.optionA: Fail secure: the doors stay locked so equipment remains protected until power is restored.
compare.optionB: Fail safe: the doors unlock so people can leave, with guards and alarms covering the assets.
compare.why: Human life takes priority over asset protection, so exit doors must fail safe. Fail secure is the tempting runner-up because it protects equipment, but it can trap people and breaches life-safety rules.

compare.scenario: A retiring team's laptops held restricted customer data on solid-state drives. The company wants to reuse the laptops internally. Which sanitization method is better?
compare.optionA: Purge the drives with cryptographic erase or the drive's secure erase command, then verify.
compare.optionB: Degauss the drives so that all magnetic data is destroyed.
compare.why: Cryptographic or secure erase purges flash storage and allows reuse. Degaussing is the tempting runner-up for sensitive data, but it has no effect on solid-state memory and also ruins magnetic drives for reuse.

compare.scenario: A company wants to protect system administrators against credential phishing, including attacker sites that relay one-time codes in real time. Which authentication method is better?
compare.optionA: A FIDO2 hardware security key that cryptographically binds the login to the genuine site.
compare.optionB: A time-based one-time passcode from an authenticator app in addition to the password.
compare.why: A FIDO2 key refuses to answer for a look-alike site, so relay phishing fails. The authenticator-app code is the tempting runner-up because it is real MFA, but a user can still type it into a fake page that forwards it instantly.

compare.scenario: Network engineers need to log in to routers and switches, and the security team wants per-command authorization and encryption of the whole session payload. Which protocol should the central AAA server use?
compare.optionA: RADIUS, because it is widely supported and combines authentication with authorization.
compare.optionB: TACACS+, because it separates the three AAA functions and encrypts the entire payload.
compare.why: TACACS+ gives per-command authorization and full payload encryption. RADIUS is the tempting runner-up because almost everything supports it, but it encrypts only the password and bundles authentication with authorization, so command-level control is limited.

compare.scenario: The patch team must verify which servers are missing security updates and wants the fewest false positives. Which scan approach is better?
compare.optionA: A credentialed scan that logs in and reads the installed patch levels and configuration.
compare.optionB: A non-credentialed scan run from the internet to mimic an external attacker.
compare.why: Authenticated scanning reads actual patch state from inside the system. The external scan is the tempting runner-up because it shows what an attacker sees, but it infers patch levels from banners and responses, which produces more false positives and negatives.

compare.scenario: An analyst has two vulnerabilities, both scored 9.8. One is on an internet-facing customer portal and is actively exploited in the wild. The other is on an isolated lab system with no data. Which remediation plan is better?
compare.optionA: Fix the customer portal vulnerability first, then schedule the lab system.
compare.optionB: Fix both in the order the scanner listed them, because the scores are identical.
compare.why: Exposure, active exploitation and asset value make the portal far riskier. Following the scanner order is the tempting runner-up because the scores match, but CVSS measures technical severity, not risk in your environment.

compare.scenario: An analyst finds a server beaconing to a command-and-control host. Memory contents may show the attacker's tools. What should the analyst do first?
compare.optionA: Isolate the server from the network and capture memory and connection data.
compare.optionB: Power off the server immediately so the attacker loses access.
compare.why: Isolation stops communication and still preserves volatile evidence. Powering off is the tempting runner-up because it is fast and decisive, but it destroys memory contents and running-process evidence that the investigation needs.

compare.scenario: A hospital's patient-records system has a recovery time objective of 2 hours and a recovery point objective of 5 minutes. Which backup and recovery design is better?
compare.optionA: Continuous replication to a warm standby environment that can be activated within an hour.
compare.optionB: Nightly full backups shipped off-site and restored to new hardware when needed.
compare.why: Continuous replication meets the 5-minute data-loss limit and a warm standby meets the 2-hour restore time. Nightly backups are the tempting runner-up because they are cheaper and sound safe, but they could lose a day of data and restoring to new hardware would likely exceed the RTO.

compare.scenario: Two offices must exchange large files confidentially each night and have no shared secret yet. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Establish a session key with an asymmetric key exchange, then encrypt the files with AES.
compare.optionB: Encrypt each file directly with RSA using the recipient's public key.
compare.why: Hybrid encryption uses asymmetric cryptography to agree on a key and fast symmetric encryption for the bulk data. Pure RSA is the tempting runner-up because it needs no shared secret, but it is far too slow for large files and limited in the data size it can encrypt.

compare.scenario: A branch office needs to join the corporate network permanently over the internet, and all inter-site traffic must be confidential and authenticated. Which is the better IPsec configuration?
compare.optionA: ESP in tunnel mode between the two edge gateways.
compare.optionB: AH in transport mode between the two edge gateways.
compare.why: ESP provides encryption plus integrity, and tunnel mode encapsulates entire packets between gateways. AH is the tempting runner-up because it authenticates, but it provides no encryption and its protection of the outer header is incompatible with NAT.

compare.scenario: A team wants to stop unknown and unapproved executables from running on a set of stable, rarely changed application servers. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: Application allowlisting that permits only approved executables.
compare.optionB: A frequently updated antivirus blocklist of known malware signatures.
compare.why: Allowlisting blocks everything not explicitly approved, which suits stable servers and stops unknown malware. The blocklist is the tempting runner-up because it needs less setup, but it can only stop what is already known to be bad.
